ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, on the left side is a vertical wall, and two right-angled wedge-shaped objects a and b of the same mass are leaning against the wall at rest. a is above, and b is below; the hypotenuse directions of the two wedge-shaped objects are opposite. The external forces F1 and F2 are both perpendicular to their respective hypotenuses, and both have horizontal components that press the objects toward the wall; because the hypotenuse directions are opposite, the vertical component directions of F1 and F2 are opposite. Then reason: Let the angle between the external force and the horizontal direction be α. For a, the supporting force N1 of the wall is equal to the horizontal component of F1, that is, N1=F1 cosα; in the vertical direction, gravity mg and the vertical component of F1 together need to be balanced by the friction force of the wall, so the magnitude of the required friction force can be written as mg plus or minus F1 sinα, with the specific sign depending on the direction of the vertical component in the figure. For b, similarly N2=F2 cosα, but because the wedge-shaped object is reversed, the direction of the vertical component of F2 is opposite to that of F1, so the wall friction force required by b is different from that of a, and may even be in the opposite direction. The condition for being at rest only requires that the magnitude of the required friction force not exceed the maximum static friction force, that is, |required vertical friction force|≤μN. If F1=F2=F is taken, then N1=N2=F cosα; although the magnitudes of the friction forces required by the two objects are different, as long as the wall is sufficiently rough, both can satisfy the static friction condition. Therefore, the equilibrium condition does not necessarily require F1 to be greater than F2 or F1 to be less than F2; the magnitudes of the two can be equal.
